Exploring and aggregating diet data

Source: vignettes/articles/exploration.Rmd
exploration.Rmd

This article covers the functions you use before drawing a diet: a few descriptive summaries, a prey accumulation curve, the classical frequency of occurrence, aggregation of rare prey to a stated threshold, and export of a stomach-by-prey matrix. It runs on the public ICES stomach data that ship with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet), prepared with the standard set-up used throughout the documentation.

library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

1. Describe the sample first

dv_summary() gives, for each predator, the number of stomachs and prey records, the number of distinct prey taxa and the mean number of records per stomach. Pass by to break it down by a covariate.

s <- dv_summary(prep)
s$total_weight <- round(s$total_weight)
s
#>            predator_common n_stomachs n_records n_taxa records_per_stomach
#> 1        Atlantic mackerel       1048      1593     10                1.52
#> 2             Atlantic cod        991      2304    144                2.32
#> 3                  Whiting        892      1605    101                1.80
#> 4          European plaice        729      1890     69                2.59
#> 5  Atlantic horse mackerel        135       245     24                1.81
#> 6            European hake        106       154     23                1.45
#> 7              Tub gurnard         90       187     37                2.08
#> 8             Thorny skate         48       184     27                3.83
#> 9                   Turbot         47        87     21                1.85
#> 10                   Brill         26        51     15                1.96
#> 11                  Angler         20        37     11                1.85
#> 12            Grey gurnard         20        30      8                1.50
#> 13             Spotted ray         15        51     10                3.40
#> 14              Cuckoo ray         13        37      8                2.85
#> 15           Thornback ray         12        28      8                2.33
#> 16           Spiny dogfish         11        15      7                1.36
#> 17                 Pollack          9        17      8                1.89
#> 18                    Ling          4         4      4                1.00
#> 19        Atlantic halibut          2         4      3                2.00
#> 20              Blonde ray          2         3      2                1.50
#> 21           Smooth-hounds          1         1      1                1.00
#> 22     Starry smooth-hound          1         3      2                3.00
#>    total_weight
#> 1          2064
#> 2         10227
#> 3          2028
#> 4          1021
#> 5           105
#> 6          1863
#> 7           711

#> 9           766

The sample is very uneven: four predators (mackerel, cod, whiting and plaice) hold 87% of the stomachs, and 10 of the 22 predators have fewer than 20 stomachs. Read every statistic for those last ones as anecdote.

By default a taxon is the finest name reached, so “Decapoda” and Crangon crangon count as two even though the second is a decapod. Read that count as the number of distinct prey names, not as species richness. Pass rank to count taxa at one stated rank, unidentified records excluded:

head(dv_summary(prep, rank = "family")[, c("predator_common", "n_stomachs", "n_taxa")], 4)
#>     predator_common n_stomachs n_taxa
#> 1 Atlantic mackerel       1048      3
#> 2      Atlantic cod        991     67
#> 3           Whiting        892     39
#> 4   European plaice        729     37

Cod has 144 distinct prey names but 67 families. Mackerel, with the largest number of stomachs, has only 10 prey names: most of its records are “Unidentified material”, “Crustacea”, “Pisces” or sandeels (Ammodytidae).

A table of prey records holds only stomachs that contained something, so it cannot give the share of empty stomachs. That has to come from the full list of stomachs examined, which the package ships as ices_stomachs:

# % of sampled stomachs flagged empty
e <- tapply(ices_stomachs$stomach_empty %in% 1, ices_stomachs$predator_common, mean)
round(100 * e[c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")], 1)
#>      Atlantic cod Atlantic mackerel   European plaice           Whiting 
#>               3.3               0.3              30.1              12.3

2. Is the diet adequately sampled?

dv_prey_accumulation() builds the cumulative prey curve: the number of prey taxa found against the number of stomachs examined, averaged over random orders of the stomachs. A curve that levels off means more stomachs would add few new taxa; a curve still rising means the sample is not yet enough.

Count taxa at one stated rank. With the finest names, a curve rises each time a new coarse name (“Crustacea”, “Decapoda”) appears next to the species already seen, and the rise grows with digestion. Here, family:

four <- c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")
acc <- dv_prey_accumulation(prep, by = spec$predator, rank = "family",
                            permutations = 50, seed = 1)
acc <- acc[acc$predator_common %in% four, ]

plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(acc$n_stomachs)), ylim = c(0, max(acc$mean_richness)),
     xlab = "Stomachs examined", ylab = "Cumulative prey families",
     main = "Prey accumulation at family rank")
cols <- c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728")
for (i in seq_along(four)) {
  a <- acc[acc$predator_common == four[i], ]
  lines(a$n_stomachs, a$mean_richness, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", legend = four, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# families gained over the last 100 stomachs of each curve
sapply(split(acc, acc$predator_common), function(a) {
  n <- nrow(a)
  round(a$mean_richness[n] - a$mean_richness[n - 100], 1)
})
#>      Atlantic cod Atlantic mackerel   European plaice           Whiting 
#>               1.9               0.0               2.0               1.2

The cod, whiting and plaice curves are still rising slowly at the full sample size: the last 100 stomachs add one or two families each. The mackerel curve is flat, but not because the mackerel diet is well sampled: almost nothing in its stomachs was identified to family. A flat curve says that more stomachs, read the same way, would add few new families; it says nothing about what better identification would add.

Keep permutations low while exploring and raise it for a figure. The seed is used for that call only.

3. Frequency of occurrence (%FO)

dv_build_tree() gives pct_occ, the share of prey records. Shares of records add up across the ranks, which is what lets them be drawn as a sunburst, but they are not the frequency of occurrence of the diet literature. dv_fo_table() computes %FO: the share of non-empty stomachs that contain each taxon, computed separately at each rank, as recommended for comparison between studies (Buckland et al., 2017).

fo <- dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "class", by = spec$predator)
head(fo[fo$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ], 6)
#>    predator_common  rank        taxon n_stomachs n_total pct_fo
#> 11    Atlantic cod class Malacostraca        618     991  62.36
#> 12    Atlantic cod class    Teleostei        332     991  33.50
#> 13    Atlantic cod class           NA        323     991  32.59
#> 14    Atlantic cod class   Polychaeta        136     991  13.72
#> 15    Atlantic cod class  Ophiuroidea         49     991   4.94
#> 16    Atlantic cod class     Bivalvia         28     991   2.83

Crustaceans (Malacostraca) occur in 62.36% of the non-empty cod stomachs and fish (Teleostei) in 33.5%. The same classes are 43.4% and 27.1% of the cod’s prey records. The two quantities answer different questions (how many fish ate it, and how much of the recorded material it is) and should be reported under their own names. The column n_total is the number of non-empty stomachs in the group: the denominator of %FO.

%FO does not add up across ranks: a parent’s %FO is computed from the stomachs that contain it, not summed from its children, and the NA row (stomachs holding at least one record not identified to class) overlaps the others. Leave rank = NULL to stack every rank.

4. Aggregating rare prey to a stated threshold

By default DietView keeps each record at the deepest rank it reached. To make the reporting resolution a stated choice, dv_aggregate_threshold() moves prey found in fewer than threshold stomachs up to their parent, and repeats up the hierarchy until every category it reports occurs in at least threshold stomachs.

Choosing the threshold

The threshold is a judgement, so look at what it costs before you fix it. dv_threshold_sweep() runs the aggregation for several values and reports the number of categories left and the share of records whose category is coarser than species:

sw <- dv_threshold_sweep(prep, thresholds = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100))
sw
#>   threshold n_categories pct_coarser
#> 1         5          110       83.28
#> 2        10           81       84.29
#> 3        20           57       86.17
#> 4        30           42       88.19
#> 5        50           32       89.60
#> 6       100           23       94.19

The share of records above species is high whatever the threshold (83.28% at 5 stomachs), because most records were never identified to species. Raising the threshold from 5 to 20 stomachs halves the number of categories (110 to 57) and moves only 2.9 more percent of the records to a coarser rank; beyond 50 the categories become broad groups. We use 20 stomachs here: about 0.5% of the 4,222 stomachs, enough for a category to be compared between the main predators, and a point where the sweep has removed most of the rare names at little cost. State the value and the reason in your methods; a different question (a per-predator description, a rare-prey study) would justify a different one.

The aggregated data 

agg <- dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, threshold = 20)
attr(agg, "aggregation")$n_categories
#> [1] 57
head(sort(table(agg$data$prey_category), decreasing = TRUE), 12)
#> 
#>     Decapoda (other)     Chordata (other)   Arthropoda (other) 
#>                  798                  721                  664 
#>   Polychaeta (other)  Ophiuroidea (other)  Ammodytidae (other) 
#>                  498                  439                  364 
#>      Crangon crangon             Bivalvia    Amphipoda (other) 
#>                  326                  317                  249 
#>     Gobiidae (other) Merlangius merlangus         Aphia minuta 
#>                  188                  170                  154
table(agg$data$prey_rank, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>   class  family   genus kingdom   order  phylum species    <NA> 
#>    1522    1047     389      39    1310    1490    1180    1553

A category named after a taxon that also has retained descendants holds only the records that stayed at that taxon, and its label ends in “(other)”. “Decapoda (other)” holds the decapods that are not in a retained family, genus or species of their own: the many records named only “Brachyura”, “Caridea” or “Decapoda”, and rare decapods merged into them. Named species such as Crangon crangon (brown shrimp), Merlangius merlangus (whiting eaten by other fish) and Aphia minuta (transparent goby) are frequent enough to stay on their own. The 1,553 records with no prey placement at all stay unidentified (NA).

The result is a dietview_prep again: ranks finer than the rank each record settled at are set to NA, so it goes straight back into the usual functions, and the sunburst then has no category rarer than the threshold.

tree_agg <- dv_build_tree(agg$data[agg$data$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ],
                          agg$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(tree_agg, mode = "occurrence", colors = dv_palette_tree(tree_agg),
            title = "Atlantic cod, prey aggregated to 20 stomachs",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")

Two arguments give three ways of counting:

dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20)                      # all predators pooled
dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20, min_predators = 2)   # pooled, and in at least 2 predators
dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20, scope = "per_predator")

The per-predator scope counts stomachs within each predator, so a prey must reach the threshold in one predator’s own stomachs. A prey found in 15 cod and 10 whiting stomachs keeps its category in the pooled tree but is merged upward in both predator trees. That leaves fewer categories at the same threshold:

dv_threshold_sweep(prep, thresholds = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50), scope = "per_predator")
#>   threshold n_categories pct_coarser
#> 1         5           98       84.83
#> 2        10           74       86.81
#> 3        20           46       90.33
#> 4        30           31       93.93
#> 5        50           28       94.42

DietView stops at the aggregation. If you summarize a statistic across several thresholds, do it in your own analysis.

5. Handing over to multivariate analysis

dv_matrix() turns the records into the stomach-by-prey matrix that ordination, PERMANOVA and compositional regression expect. If you aggregated first, it uses the prey_category column automatically. Pass rank to build the matrix at one rank instead.

m <- dv_matrix(agg, currency = "weight")
dim(m)
#> [1] 4222   58
m[1:3, c("Crangon crangon", "Decapoda (other)", "Chordata (other)", "NA")]
#>         Crangon crangon Decapoda (other) Chordata (other) NA
#> S107497               0                0            1.394  0
#> S107498               0                0            1.505  0
#> S107499               0                0            0.000  0

One row per stomach (4,222), one column per category (58, the NA column included), summed prey weight in each cell. The matrix is very sparse: 97.2% of its cells are zero, which is typical of stomach data and matters for the choice of distance in the analysis that follows.

currency is "weight" (summed weight), "occurrence" (number of records) or "fo" (presence or absence in each unit). Use unit to sum over something coarser than a stomach, such as a haul (unit = "haul_id"). Use include_na = FALSE to drop the unidentified column, and say in your methods that you did.

# DietView stops here; the analysis uses other packages
mm <- vegan::decostand(m[rowSums(m) > 0, ], "total")
d  <- vegan::vegdist(mm, "bray")
# vegan::adonis2(d ~ predator_common + region, data = stomach_covariates)

Where this fits

These functions describe and aggregate. DietView does not test hypotheses: diversity tests, PERMANOVA and dispersion analyses belong to packages built for them, and dv_matrix() is the step that hands your data over.

References

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. Fisheries Research, 196, 126–140.

ICES Stomach Content Database. ICES, Copenhagen. https://stomachdata.ices.dk. Extract distributed with the R package stomachr (Lindmark 2026, https://github.com/maxlindmark/stomachr).
